source.title: Trait-space Monitoring for Emergent Misalignment During Supervised Finetuning
source.authors: Huy Nghiem; Sy-Tuyen Ho; Sarah Wiegreffe; Hal Daumé

record.tranche_reason: The study measures activation drift and tests an emergent-misalignment monitor, but it does not test feature superposition, capacity competition, or whether SAE features recover the model's underlying features. Feature superposition appears only as cited related work.
record.gate_note: The paper reports an SAE-latent baseline for predicting emergent misalignment; that evaluates monitoring utility, not feature recovery or the geometry of feature storage. Its PCA and trait-direction geometry results concern finetuning drift in alignment-trait coordinates, not superposition. The cited feature-superposition study is not a result of this paper.
record.test_reason: The study builds an emergent-misalignment monitor from contrastive trait directions and compares it with baselines, one of which is a small K=256 SAE trained on base activations. It does not test superposition, capacity competition, polysemanticity, whether SAE features recover the model's features, or feature dimensionality. Feature superposition appears only as a cited related work (Minegishi et al. 2026). The SAE result is monitor utility (FNR/AUROC for predicting EM), not feature recovery, so it fits no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that drift in a seven-trait activation space has a dominant axis (78.6% variance) and supports a checkpoint-level EM monitor (1.8% FNR, 2.0% FPR on held-out data). They add that calibration may need refreshing across architecture, update method, training horizon or starting alignment. They draw no conclusions about superposition or SAEs as canonical units.
record.recipe_differences: The paper does not reproduce or test the Toy Models of Superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Monitor performance and calibration vary with extraction prompts, layer, training update method, architecture, training horizon, and starting alignment state.

fits_no_version.finding: A per-model K=256 SAE trained on base activations, used as EM-monitor features, trails contrastive trait directions: FNR 31.8–41.9%, AUROC 0.873–0.975, versus 1.8% FNR and AUROC 0.989 for the 7D trait basis.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Small from-scratch SAE latent drift carries emergent-misalignment signal but predicts it less well than supervised contrastive trait directions; this says nothing about whether SAE latents are the model's features.

record.problems: No direct evidence addresses the claim versions. The SAE baseline is used only for EM monitoring, not assessed for feature-recovery quality or feature completeness; the SAE is trained on a limited base-activation sample.

untested.parts: All: toy-model storage of sparse features as nearly orthogonal directions, sparsity transition, geometry.
All: capacity competition as the cause of polysemanticity.
All: non-capacity origins of polysemantic neurons.
Whether LLM features are spread across neurons or recoverable by SAEs; the SAE here is only used as monitor input.
Completeness, stability or canonicity of SAE features.
One-dimensional vs multi-dimensional features. The paper's linear trait directions are assumed, not tested against multi-dimensional alternatives.

record.verdict_notes: The relation is better described as cites_only than discusses: superposition appears only as a one-line related-work citation. The SAE baseline is small (K=256), is trained on a few seconds' worth of base activations, and has no reconstruction or feature-quality metrics reported, so it cannot bear on V4 or V5. Low-dimensional drift (native PCA, top-5 components 96.9–99.5%) concerns finetuning drift, not feature superposition.

versions.untested_parts: Whether sparse features outnumbering dimensions are stored as overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions; sparsity-dependent transitions and regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity results from capacity competition or important features receiving dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
Whether LLM features are spread across neurons or whether an SAE recovers sparse features; the SAE baseline measures EM-monitor performance, not feature recovery.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of model representation.
Whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.
